creator: W&M Libraries
title: Case 1 of Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is an image of Case 1 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: ‘The Only Union Lady’ Pencil sketch of Mary Ann Bowden (age 15) drawn by a Union soldier at the time of the Battle of Williamsburg. She was the daughter of Lemuel Bowden, an ardent Unionist. It bears the note: ‘Williamsburg College Hospital.’ Bowden was installed as mayor by the United States Army. The Bowden House, now known as the Armistead House is located on Duke of Gloucester Street. Bruton Parish Church Vestry Minutes, 1865 Thomas Ambler, the rector of Bruton Parish Church, refused to say the prayer for the president of the United States as printed in the Book of Common Prayer. While the church was closed, Ambler had secret prayer meetings in his house. The church reopened briefly but was closed again in 1863. This entry shows that the church was trying to gather its property in the fall of 1865 to be able to reopen. The October 1865 entry was written recto-verso on the same leaf of paper, and for display purposes the two pages have been reproduced facing each other. Diary, 1862, of Harriette Cary Diary, kept by twenty-four year old Harriette Cary during the occupation of Williamsburg. She kept the diary for three months immediately after the Battle of Williamsburg. In June of 1862, the townspeople were caring for the Confederate wounded and reading Northern newspapers. Account, 1864, of a trip by Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman The entire peninsula from Norfolk to Williamsburg was occupied by federal forces. But the area around Richmond was still held by the Confederacy. Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman traveled from Richmond to within thirteen miles of Williamsburg to retrieve some of her belongings sent out of the occupied town by her mother. She also was able to warn Confederate troops that the Union guard at Williamsburg had been doubled and not to attack. Letters, 1862, of Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman married Doctor Charles Coleman during the Civil War. Although she was absent from Williamsburg during part of the occupation, she wrote these letters concerning the treatment of wounded Confederate prisoners in Williamsburg to Col. Campbell, a Union army officer. Busteed Order Following the Confederate Raid on Williamsburg, 29 March 1863 The raid on Williamsburg by Confederate troops, 29 March 1863, resulted in an order by Brigadier-General Richard Busteed, stating that the “attack was aided, if not planned, by citizens of Williamsburg and carried to a successful end by them . . .” and giving the punishment for the citizens. The order was countermanded the next day by Major-General John A. Dix. Lithograph, “Williamsburg Female Academy. Virginia.” Drawn by W. F. Grabau Printed by P. S. Dubal’s Steam Lith. Press, Philadelphia The Williamsburg Female Academy was incorporated in 1839 by the Virginia General Assembly. It stood where the colonial capitol does now and was used as a barrack for federal soldiers during the Union occupation of Williamsburg. Robert A. Saunders, Williamsburg, Va. to Lucy Burwell Saunders, Hanover, Va., 12 September 1862 Saunders had been president of the College of William & Mary from 1847-1848. He wrote to his wife, who had fled Williamsburg, about the excessive heat and sent her word from their slaves. John Adams Dix to Henry A. Wise, 28 April 1863 Continued harassment by Confederate troops led Union Major-General John Adams Dix to write Confederate General Henry A. Wise that, if the attacks did not stop, he would release the patients of the Eastern Lunatic Asylum (now Eastern State Hospital) onto the streets of Richmond. Minié Balls and Cannon Ball, circa 1862 The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation field crew and William & Mary field school students excavated this Civil War era ammunition in the historic campus. The cannon ball was unearthed in the Wren Yard during excavations led by Steve Archer from 2005-2007. Mark Kostro led the 2011 Brafferton dig that uncovered the Minié balls exhibited here. Sally M. Galt, Williamsburg, Va. to Col. West, 3 February, 1864 The policy of the Union army was that all citizens in an occupied territory should either take the Oath of Allegiance to the United States Government or leave the territory. Sally M. Galt wrote to protest the policy and to plead to be allowed to stay. She was permitted to remain in town. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

title: Case 2 of Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is an image of Case 2 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: Edward R. Yoder, Freedman’s Store, Yorktown, Va. to E. J. Ransom, 25 October 1864 Yoder, possibly a Quaker teacher, described a school in Yorktown, Va. for contraband (freed blacks). He mentioned helping to raise a bell into the school house that once belonged to a Yorktown church. This may have been Grace Episcopal Church whose bell was taken to Philadelphia and later returned to the congregation. Slabtown: the African-American Presence at Yorktown As soon as Yorktown (which became known as Fort Yorktown) was abandoned by Confederate forces on May 4, 1862 and occupied by Federal troops, slaves began coming into the Union lines. Although the Emancipation Proclamation, which took effect in January of 1863, did not free slaves in occupied areas such as Yorktown, blacks, referred to as contraband of war or simply contrabands, continued to flock there. In the fall of 1863, United States Colored Troops (U. S. C. T.) arrived. After Isaac Wister took command, he ordered quarters for blacks built three-quarters of a mile from Fort Yorktown. Three communities were set up: Slabtown, Acretown (now Lackey) and Slab Richmond at Gloucester Point. Shiloh Baptist Church in Lackey was founded by contrabands in 1863 and is still active today. The Quakers (Friends Freedmen Relief Association) sent supplies, tools and teachers. They also opened stores. The National Cemetery in Yorktown where the remains of U.S.C.T. soldiers are interred, is located near Slabtown. The National Park Service maintains a permanent exhibit relating to the contraband settlement in a building near the cemetery. Grace Episcopal Church Grace Episcopal Church was built in 1697 and burned in 1814. Rebuilt in 1848, it suffered damage during the Civil War. The church with the original marl walls still stands in Yorktown today. The church bell (1725) was removed, and perhaps placed in a schoolhouse where contrabands were taught. It later made its way to Philadelphia, was recast in 1882, and then returned to the church. Yorktown Artifacts Eagle breastplate, eagle uniform button and shoulder scales (a type of epaulet), all found at Yorktown. The breastplate was supposed to cover a soldier’s heart and was worn on the strap of an ammunition box that would cover the chest. The eagle insignia was indicative of the style issued to Union forces. creator: W&M Libraries
title: Case 1 of Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is an image of Case 1 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: ‘The Only Union Lady’ Pencil sketch of Mary Ann Bowden (age 15) drawn by a Union soldier at the time of the Battle of Williamsburg. She was the daughter of Lemuel Bowden, an ardent Unionist. It bears the note: ‘Williamsburg College Hospital.’ Bowden was installed as mayor by the United States Army. The Bowden House, now known as the Armistead House is located on Duke of Gloucester Street. Bruton Parish Church Vestry Minutes, 1865 Thomas Ambler, the rector of Bruton Parish Church, refused to say the prayer for the president of the United States as printed in the Book of Common Prayer. While the church was closed, Ambler had secret prayer meetings in his house. The church reopened briefly but was closed again in 1863. This entry shows that the church was trying to gather its property in the fall of 1865 to be able to reopen. The October 1865 entry was written recto-verso on the same leaf of paper, and for display purposes the two pages have been reproduced facing each other. Diary, 1862, of Harriette Cary Diary, kept by twenty-four year old Harriette Cary during the occupation of Williamsburg. She kept the diary for three months immediately after the Battle of Williamsburg. In June of 1862, the townspeople were caring for the Confederate wounded and reading Northern newspapers. Account, 1864, of a trip by Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman The entire peninsula from Norfolk to Williamsburg was occupied by federal forces. But the area around Richmond was still held by the Confederacy. Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman traveled from Richmond to within thirteen miles of Williamsburg to retrieve some of her belongings sent out of the occupied town by her mother. She also was able to warn Confederate troops that the Union guard at Williamsburg had been doubled and not to attack. Letters, 1862, of Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman married Doctor Charles Coleman during the Civil War. Although she was absent from Williamsburg during part of the occupation, she wrote these letters concerning the treatment of wounded Confederate prisoners in Williamsburg to Col. Campbell, a Union army officer. Busteed Order Following the Confederate Raid on Williamsburg, 29 March 1863 The raid on Williamsburg by Confederate troops, 29 March 1863, resulted in an order by Brigadier-General Richard Busteed, stating that the “attack was aided, if not planned, by citizens of Williamsburg and carried to a successful end by them . . .” and giving the punishment for the citizens. The order was countermanded the next day by Major-General John A. Dix. Lithograph, “Williamsburg Female Academy. Virginia.” Drawn by W. F. Grabau Printed by P. S. Dubal’s Steam Lith. Press, Philadelphia The Williamsburg Female Academy was incorporated in 1839 by the Virginia General Assembly. It stood where the colonial capitol does now and was used as a barrack for federal soldiers during the Union occupation of Williamsburg. Robert A. Saunders, Williamsburg, Va. to Lucy Burwell Saunders, Hanover, Va., 12 September 1862 Saunders had been president of the College of William & Mary from 1847-1848. He wrote to his wife, who had fled Williamsburg, about the excessive heat and sent her word from their slaves. John Adams Dix to Henry A. Wise, 28 April 1863 Continued harassment by Confederate troops led Union Major-General John Adams Dix to write Confederate General Henry A. Wise that, if the attacks did not stop, he would release the patients of the Eastern Lunatic Asylum (now Eastern State Hospital) onto the streets of Richmond. Minié Balls and Cannon Ball, circa 1862 The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation field crew and William & Mary field school students excavated this Civil War era ammunition in the historic campus. The cannon ball was unearthed in the Wren Yard during excavations led by Steve Archer from 2005-2007. Mark Kostro led the 2011 Brafferton dig that uncovered the Minié balls exhibited here. Sally M. Galt, Williamsburg, Va. to Col. West, 3 February, 1864 The policy of the Union army was that all citizens in an occupied territory should either take the Oath of Allegiance to the United States Government or leave the territory. Sally M. Galt wrote to protest the policy and to plead to be allowed to stay. She was permitted to remain in town. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

Yoder, Freedman’s Store, Yorktown, Va. to E. J. Ransom, 25 October 1864 Yoder, possibly a Quaker teacher, described a school in Yorktown, Va. for contraband (freed blacks). He mentioned helping to raise a bell into the school house that once belonged to a Yorktown church. This may have been Grace Episcopal Church whose bell was taken to Philadelphia and later returned to the congregation. Slabtown: the African-American Presence at Yorktown As soon as Yorktown (which became known as Fort Yorktown) was abandoned by Confederate forces on May 4, 1862 and occupied by Federal troops, slaves began coming into the Union lines. Although the Emancipation Proclamation, which took effect in January of 1863, did not free slaves in occupied areas such as Yorktown, blacks, referred to as contraband of war or simply contrabands, continued to flock there. In the fall of 1863, United States Colored Troops (U. S. C. T.) arrived. After Isaac Wister took command, he ordered quarters for blacks built three-quarters of a mile from Fort Yorktown. Three communities were set up: Slabtown, Acretown (now Lackey) and Slab Richmond at Gloucester Point. Shiloh Baptist Church in Lackey was founded by contrabands in 1863 and is still active today. The Quakers (Friends Freedmen Relief Association) sent supplies, tools and teachers. They also opened stores. The National Cemetery in Yorktown where the remains of U.S.C.T. soldiers are interred, is located near Slabtown. The National Park Service maintains a permanent exhibit relating to the contraband settlement in a building near the cemetery. Grace Episcopal Church Grace Episcopal Church was built in 1697 and burned in 1814. Rebuilt in 1848, it suffered damage during the Civil War. The church with the original marl walls still stands in Yorktown today. The church bell (1725) was removed, and perhaps placed in a schoolhouse where contrabands were taught. It later made its way to Philadelphia, was recast in 1882, and then returned to the church. Yorktown Artifacts Eagle breastplate, eagle uniform button and shoulder scales (a type of epaulet), all found at Yorktown. The breastplate was supposed to cover a soldier’s heart and was worn on the strap of an ammunition box that would cover the chest. The eagle insignia was indicative of the style issued to Union forces. It was printed on the press of the Weekly Gazette and Eastern Virginia Advertiser Weekly Review. The letter of John A. Dix to Henry A. Wise was not only printed in the Cavalier, but also received wide circulation in Northern papers. Business is Booming in Yorktown The federal occupation of the port town led to small businesses springing up to serve the troops. Advertisements were published in the Cavalier, a paper printed by the troops. John Jacob Astor Telegram, 4 May 1862 John Jacob Astor served as aide-de-camp to Gen. George McClellan. Immensely wealthy, he moved to England after the war. In this telegram from Yorktown, he signaled that the rebel army had evacuated Yorktown, leaving eighty cannons behind. This evacuation would pave the way for the occupation of the town, made famous by Cornwallis’s surrender in 1781. Aerial View of Jamestown, 1998 While there was no engagement at Jamestown, it was considered a strategic defense point on the James River and, after Confederate forces abandoned it, it was occupied for the remainder of the war by Union troops. But for a brief time, no military presence was there and in late summer or early autumn of 1862, the Ambler House at Jamestown was burned by former slaves. The ruins are still visible today. Murder at Jamestown, October 1862 Jacob Morton Shriver, the uncle of Mrs. William Allen (wife of the owner of Jamestown Island) and two blacks, Littleton (slave) and Gilbert Wooten (free black) went to Jamestown along with Joseph A. Graves and his nephew George Graves (child). Seven armed slaves (formerly owned by Allen) first captured Wooten and later the rest of Wooten’s party. A crowd of about 100 blacks gathered. Joseph Graves, George Graves, Shriver, and Wooten were shot. Wooten, though shot three times, escaped, but the others were killed. title: Case 1 of Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is an image of Case 1 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: ‘The Only Union Lady’ Pencil sketch of Mary Ann Bowden (age 15) drawn by a Union soldier at the time of the Battle of Williamsburg. She was the daughter of Lemuel Bowden, an ardent Unionist. It bears the note: ‘Williamsburg College Hospital.’ Bowden was installed as mayor by the United States Army. The Bowden House, now known as the Armistead House is located on Duke of Gloucester Street. Bruton Parish Church Vestry Minutes, 1865 Thomas Ambler, the rector of Bruton Parish Church, refused to say the prayer for the president of the United States as printed in the Book of Common Prayer. While the church was closed, Ambler had secret prayer meetings in his house. The church reopened briefly but was closed again in 1863. This entry shows that the church was trying to gather its property in the fall of 1865 to be able to reopen. The October 1865 entry was written recto-verso on the same leaf of paper, and for display purposes the two pages have been reproduced facing each other. Diary, 1862, of Harriette Cary Diary, kept by twenty-four year old Harriette Cary during the occupation of Williamsburg. She kept the diary for three months immediately after the Battle of Williamsburg. In June of 1862, the townspeople were caring for the Confederate wounded and reading Northern newspapers. Account, 1864, of a trip by Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman The entire peninsula from Norfolk to Williamsburg was occupied by federal forces. But the area around Richmond was still held by the Confederacy. Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman traveled from Richmond to within thirteen miles of Williamsburg to retrieve some of her belongings sent out of the occupied town by her mother. She also was able to warn Confederate troops that the Union guard at Williamsburg had been doubled and not to attack. Letters, 1862, of Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman Cynthia Beverley Tucker Washington Coleman married Doctor Charles Coleman during the Civil War. Although she was absent from Williamsburg during part of the occupation, she wrote these letters concerning the treatment of wounded Confederate prisoners in Williamsburg to Col. Campbell, a Union army officer. Busteed Order Following the Confederate Raid on Williamsburg, 29 March 1863 The raid on Williamsburg by Confederate troops, 29 March 1863, resulted in an order by Brigadier-General Richard Busteed, stating that the “attack was aided, if not planned, by citizens of Williamsburg and carried to a successful end by them . . .” and giving the punishment for the citizens. The order was countermanded the next day by Major-General John A. Dix. Lithograph, “Williamsburg Female Academy. Virginia.” Drawn by W. F. Grabau Printed by P. S. Dubal’s Steam Lith. Press, Philadelphia The Williamsburg Female Academy was incorporated in 1839 by the Virginia General Assembly. It stood where the colonial capitol does now and was used as a barrack for federal soldiers during the Union occupation of Williamsburg. Robert A. Saunders, Williamsburg, Va. to Lucy Burwell Saunders, Hanover, Va., 12 September 1862 Saunders had been president of the College of William & Mary from 1847-1848. He wrote to his wife, who had fled Williamsburg, about the excessive heat and sent her word from their slaves. John Adams Dix to Henry A. Wise, 28 April 1863 Continued harassment by Confederate troops led Union Major-General John Adams Dix to write Confederate General Henry A. Wise that, if the attacks did not stop, he would release the patients of the Eastern Lunatic Asylum (now Eastern State Hospital) onto the streets of Richmond. Minié Balls and Cannon Ball, circa 1862 The Colonial Williamsburg Foundation field crew and William & Mary field school students excavated this Civil War era ammunition in the historic campus. The cannon ball was unearthed in the Wren Yard during excavations led by Steve Archer from 2005-2007. Mark Kostro led the 2011 Brafferton dig that uncovered the Minié balls exhibited here. Sally M. Galt, Williamsburg, Va. to Col. West, 3 February, 1864 The policy of the Union army was that all citizens in an occupied territory should either take the Oath of Allegiance to the United States Government or leave the territory. Sally M. Galt wrote to protest the policy and to plead to be allowed to stay. She was permitted to remain in town. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

title: Label from Case 2 of the Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle
description: Shown here is a label from Case 2 of the "Under the Shield: The Federal Occupation of the Historic Triangle" Exhibit located in the Marshall Gallery (1st Floor Rotunda) of Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from February 7th 2013 to August 13th 2013 The following is a transcription of the label text: Slabtown: the African-American Presence at Yorktown As soon as Yorktown (which became known as Fort Yorktown) was abandoned by Confederate forces on May 4, 1862 and occupied by Federal troops, slaves began coming into the Union lines. Although the Emancipation Proclamation, which took effect in January of 1863, did not free slaves in occupied areas such as Yorktown, blacks, referred to as contraband of war or simply contrabands, continued to flock there. In the fall of 1863, United States Colored Troops (U. S. C. T.) arrived. After Isaac Wister took command, he ordered quarters for blacks built three-quarters of a mile from Fort Yorktown. Three communities were set up: Slabtown, Acretown (now Lackey) and Slab Richmond at Gloucester Point. Shiloh Baptist Church in Lackey was founded by contrabands in 1863 and is still active today. The Quakers (Friends Freedmen Relief Association) sent supplies, tools and teachers. They also opened stores. The National Cemetery in Yorktown where the remains of U.S.C.T. soldiers are interred, is located near Slabtown. The National Park Service maintains a permanent exhibit relating to the contraband settlement in a building near the cemetery. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

Graves and his nephew George Graves (child). Seven armed slaves (formerly owned by Allen) first captured Wooten and later the rest of Wooten’s party. A crowd of about 100 blacks gathered. Joseph Graves, George Graves, Shriver, and Wooten were shot. Wooten, though shot three times, escaped, but the others were killed. description: Shown here is a label from Case 1 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War, an Exhibit located in the Special Collections Research Center Lobby in Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from April 17th 2013 to October 16th 2013 The following is a transcription of the label text: School Different types of schools, including boarding and subscription schools, existed during the Civil War. The tuition usually funded the schoolmaster’s salary. Levels of rigor varied as did the quality of the instructional materials. Textbooks at that time were called “primers.” As the war continued, the Confederacy sought to provide its own primers. The cover of one of those depicts the Sir Christopher Wren Building at the College of William & Mary. Two schools are presented in this case: New England’s Willis School, attended by Lizzie Ladd and Williamsburg’s Galt School. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

During and after the war many benevolent organizations began to care for children without parents or extended families. From ‘Orphan Trains’ that took children from the East out West, to the creation of Soldiers’ Orphans Homes, charities assisted more than 100,000 children in need. One such orphanage was the Burd Orphan Asylum in Pennsylvania which was founded by the estate of Eliza Burd. Here, preference was given to orphaned daughters of clergy men. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

Mourning dress, photos, and jewelry were commonplace. And men in the field missed those from whom the war had separated them. They longed to be home with their families and often expressed these sentiments in diaries and letters. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

These illnesses spread more quickly with the migration of people during the war. The occurrence of diseases also likely increased due to other war-related factors like malnutrition. The two letters in this case from Ann Maury to her niece Nan and from Nannie Watkins to her husband show the impact of childhood illness. The reference to “[w]hooping cough” is matter of fact, probably because it was a common childhood illness at the time; while on the other hand, little Charley’s death from fever was unexpected and his mother’s letter indicates a commitment to her Christian faith in dealing with her sudden loss. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

A very popular book series for children and young adults was “Peter Parley,” written primarily by Samuel and Charles Goodrich. Examples of these children’s books are provided throughout this case. And like many of us, the children back then may very well have doodled in their own, or their parents’ books. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

title: Case 2 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War
description: Shown here is an image of Case 2 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War, an Exhibit located in the Special Collections Research Center Lobby in Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from April 17th 2013 to October 16th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: Childhood Illness and Death Child mortality during the Civil War was high due to outbreaks of diseases such as whooping cough, scarlet fever and yellow fever. These illnesses spread more quickly with the migration of people during the war. The occurrence of diseases also likely increased due to other war-related factors like malnutrition. The two letters in this case from Ann Maury to her niece Nan and from Nannie Watkins to her husband show the impact of childhood illness. The reference to “[w]hooping cough” is matter of fact, probably because it was a common childhood illness at the time; while on the other hand, little Charley’s death from fever was unexpected and his mother’s letter indicates a commitment to her Christian faith in dealing with her sudden loss. Mourning and Separation With the number of casualties exceeding half a million, families were significantly impacted by the Civil War, and worry, loss, and mourning were frequent occurrences. Mourning dress, photos, and jewelry were commonplace. And men in the field missed those from whom the war had separated them. They longed to be home with their families and often expressed these sentiments in diaries and letters. Orphans The Civil War increased the number of orphans and highlighted their plight. During and after the war many benevolent organizations began to care for children without parents or extended families. From ‘Orphan Trains’ that took children from the East out West, to the creation of Soldiers’ Orphans Homes, charities assisted more than 100,000 children in need. One such orphanage was the Burd Orphan Asylum in Pennsylvania which was founded by the estate of Eliza Burd. Here, preference was given to orphaned daughters of clergy men. description: Shown here is an image of Case 1 of Blockades, Books, and Bassinets: Children playing, learning, and surviving during the Civil War, an Exhibit located in the Special Collections Research Center Lobby in Swem Library at the College of William & Mary, on display from April 17th 2013 to October 16th 2013 The following is a transcription of the labels in this case: Play and Mischief Even during the war, children enjoyed playing: boys likely played soldiers, and girls enjoyed dolls and dress up games (fans & jewelry included, and possibly not allowed). In addition to playing, children (shockingly) misbehaved. Two such examples: Willie who decided to stay out too late and got into trouble and Charley, who according to his mother was “very bad.” Reading (and Doodling) Reading was an important skill (although many children remained illiterate) and once acquired, older children may have continued to learn about life, customs, and current events through the written word, specifically almanacs and newspapers. A very popular book series for children and young adults was “Peter Parley,” written primarily by Samuel and Charles Goodrich. Examples of these children’s books are provided throughout this case. And like many of us, the children back then may very well have doodled in their own, or their parents’ books. Learning Learning, whether at home or in school, was important for children. From reading to history to music to ciphering, learning about manners and cultivating friendships as well as assisting with younger siblings and simply using one’s imagination, were all parts of this process. Like today, childhood friendships could sometimes be fraught with drama. Sarah “Lizzie” Ladd did not share what offense her friend Nell may have been guilty of, just simply her displeasure. Siblings (surprisingly) did not always get along. In this letter, his father instructs young Charley to mind his mother and not make his sister cry. School Different types of schools, including boarding and subscription schools, existed during the Civil War. The tuition usually funded the schoolmaster’s salary. Levels of rigor varied as did the quality of the instructional materials. Textbooks at that time were called “primers.” As the war continued, the Confederacy sought to provide its own primers. The cover of one of those depicts the Sir Christopher Wren Building at the College of William & Mary. Two schools are presented in this case: New England’s Willis School, attended by Lizzie Ladd and Williamsburg’s Galt School. A New Normal While children still played, misbehaved, learned, and made friends, they also faced separation from family, hunger, and other challenges associated with the war. In this exchange of letters between Charley and his father Nathaniel, the attempts of parent and child to stay connected evoke emotions that transcend time. Clothed and Fed Picking lint for dressing wounds, knitting socks, and other efforts to assist soldiers near and far became everyday occurrences at home. Efforts to keep children clothed and shoed depended greatly upon location and resources. A tale of contrasts, even from early in the war, is depicted by these two accounts: a letter from Ann Maury (Union) and the diary of Charles Campbell (Confederate). In the South, especially, inflation was rampant and by war’s end, food and cloth were extremely expensive and often scarce; it likely took much time, money, and pluck to fill this market bag even with basic supplies. From the Special Collections Research Center, Earl Gregg Swem Library at the College of William and Mary. See swem.wm.edu/research/special-collections for further information and assistance.

They beat the drums of war, but also filled canteens, assisted with horses, and tended to the wounded. Like today, childhood friendships could sometimes be fraught with drama. Sarah “Lizzie” Ladd did not share what offense her friend Nell may have been guilty of, just simply her displeasure. Siblings (surprisingly) did not always get along. In this letter, his father instructs young Charley to mind his mother and not make his sister cry. School Different types of schools, including boarding and subscription schools, existed during the Civil War. The tuition usually funded the schoolmaster’s salary. Levels of rigor varied as did the quality of the instructional materials. Textbooks at that time were called “primers.” As the war continued, the Confederacy sought to provide its own primers. The cover of one of those depicts the Sir Christopher Wren Building at the College of William & Mary. Two schools are presented in this case: New England’s Willis School, attended by Lizzie Ladd and Williamsburg’s Galt School. A New Normal While children still played, misbehaved, learned, and made friends, they also faced separation from family, hunger, and other challenges associated with the war. In this exchange of letters between Charley and his father Nathaniel, the attempts of parent and child to stay connected evoke emotions that transcend time. Clothed and Fed Picking lint for dressing wounds, knitting socks, and other efforts to assist soldiers near and far became everyday occurrences at home. Efforts to keep children clothed and shoed depended greatly upon location and resources. A tale of contrasts, even from early in the war, is depicted by these two accounts: a letter from Ann Maury (Union) and the diary of Charles Campbell (Confederate). In the South, especially, inflation was rampant and by war’s end, food and cloth were extremely expensive and often scarce; it likely took much time, money, and pluck to fill this market bag even with basic supplies.
